What this place is

Half coffeehouse. Half general store. Entirely Enumclaw.

Most towns have a coffee shop. Most towns used to have a general store. We couldn't decide which one Enumclaw needed more, so we built both into the same room — a place where you can order a cortado, find a gift, admire a painting by somebody who lives twelve minutes away, and lose an afternoon to a chess board.

Pull up a chair

How it started

Two friends, seventeen years of coffee, one good idea.

Amy Lundeen and Beckie Kahne met over a cup of coffee seventeen years before they ever unlocked a door on Cole Street. They stayed close through all of it — jobs, moves, kids, the ordinary weather of a long friendship. They stood up in each other's weddings.

So when the two of them finally decided to build something together, it was never really in question what it would be. It would be the thing that had been sitting between them the whole time.

Seventeen years of conversations over coffee. It seemed only fair to build somewhere for everyone else to have theirs.

The shelves

A general store, in the old sense of it.

Candles, ceramics, cards, small-batch pantry things, the odd item you didn't know existed until you picked it up. We lean hard toward makers in Washington, because a general store that stocks the same things as everywhere else isn't really a general store — it's just a shelf.

Our story

It started, as these things do, over a cup of coffee.

Seventeen years of them, actually — long before there was ever a shop on Cole Street to sit in.

  • Hours on the visit page
  • Doors opened June 4, 2015

Amy & Beckie

Two friends, and a very long conversation.

Amy Lundeen and Beckie Kahne met over a cup of coffee seventeen years before they ever unlocked a door on Cole Street. What started as one conversation turned into the kind of friendship that survives everything ordinary life throws at it — jobs, moves, kids, the whole weather system of seventeen years.

They stood up in each other's weddings. They kept meeting for coffee.

So when the two of them finally decided to build something together, the shape of it was never really in question. It would be the thing that had been sitting on the table between them the entire time.

Seventeen years of conversations over coffee. It seemed only fair to build somewhere for everyone else to have theirs.

Why a general store

Enumclaw didn't need another coffee shop. It needed this.

There were places to get a coffee. What there wasn't — not anymore, not really — was the kind of room a town used to have. The one where you could pick up a gift, run into three people you know, look at something made by somebody who lives nearby, and stay a while without anybody hovering.

That room used to be called the general store. We just added an espresso machine and kept the rest.

Since 2015

How it went

Eleven years on Cole Street.

  1. 1998

    A first cup of coffee

    Amy and Beckie meet. Neither of them is thinking about opening anything.

  2. 2015

    The doors open

    June 4th. A general store and coffeehouse at 1616 Cole Street, with Stumptown on the bar and Washington-made goods on the shelves from day one.

  3. Since

    The room fills up

    Regulars by name. Local artists on the walls, and their work going home with people. Meetings, first dates, laptops, chess games, and a lot of mornings that start at six.

  4. Today

    Still here, still opening early

    Seven days a week. Same corner, same idea.

What we believe

Local isn't a marketing word here. It's the buying policy.

If it's made in Washington, it goes on the shelf first. If the artist lives nearby, their work goes on the wall — and the price tag has their name on it, not ours. It costs more and it takes longer, and it is the entire reason this place is called what it's called.

The store

The other half of the room.

A general store in the old sense — a little of what you need, a lot of what you didn't know you wanted, and as much of it made in Washington as we can get our hands on.

  • Hours on the visit page
  • The stock turns over constantly

Why we stock it this way

If it's made down the road, it goes on the shelf first.

There's no shortage of places to buy a candle. What's harder to find is the one poured by somebody two towns over, in a batch of forty, by a person whose name we know. That's the shelf we're trying to build — and it's why the inventory shifts constantly. Come in twice in a month and you'll find different things.

Pantry & small batch

Jams, honey, syrups, seasonings and the sort of things that make a good gift basket look effortless.

Home & hearth

Candles, ceramics, textiles and small wooden things. The woodsy, warm, quiet end of the shelf.

Cards & curiosities

Greeting cards, stationery, and the knick knacks you pick up, put down, and then come back for.

Art on the walls

Original work by artists who live here. It's not decoration — every piece on the wall is for sale, and the artist gets the credit.

by hand

Makers & artists

Everything on these walls belongs to somebody who lives here.

The art isn't decoration and the shelves aren't a catalog. Both are the work of people from around here — and both are for sale.

How it works

Simple, and deliberately so.

You make something in Washington. We put it on the shelf or hang it on the wall, with your name on the tag. Somebody buys it, and the credit — and the conversation about who made it — goes to you. That's the whole arrangement.

1 · Bring us a sample

Walk in with it. Genuinely — the best things on these shelves arrived exactly that way, in somebody's hands on a Tuesday.

2 · We'll talk it through

What you make, how much of it you can make, and what it should cost. No forms, no portal, no waiting on a committee.

3 · It goes out front

On the shelf or on the wall, tagged with your name and where you're from. We'll tell people about it, because that's half the point.

On the wall, on the shelf

What's here today came from somebody nearby.

We can't keep a permanent list on a page — the whole thing turns over as makers come and go. So here's what's true no matter what's out when you walk in.

The wall

Original work by artists who live around here, hung where you can stand in front of it with a coffee. All of it is for sale. If a piece stops you on your way to a table, ask us about it.

The shelves

Washington-made goods, in whatever quantity the people making them can manage. Which is why the shelf looks different from one visit to the next — and why we can't promise the thing you bought last time is still here.

The tag

Whatever you pick up, the tag says who made it. The credit goes to them, not to us. Ask at the counter and we'll tell you the rest of it.

Made something?

We'd like to see it.

If you paint, throw, pour, bake, stitch, carve or otherwise make something with your hands in Washington — come in and bring it. Some of the best conversations we have start exactly that way.
